metadata.title: Animate the Warburg Effect with Claude Code

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — open on the Claude UI, ask shown answered
beats.narration_text: Hola, Liam. One Claude prompt. An animated Warburg effect — one glucose, two destinations, and the size gap that explains why cancer cells look hungry even when they're fed.

props.command: claude "Port the warburg-carbon plate from plates_gen.py p03() into Manim. Hexagon input, two tracks: upper (VERM nodes) ends in large ATP square, lower (GREEN nodes) ends in building blocks + small ATP square."

beats.role_note: The mechanism before the build — two fates of glucose
beats.narration_text: Normal cells burn glucose completely — full oxidation, thirty ATP per glucose, maximum energy. Cancer cells mostly skip that and run glycolysis even in oxygen. This plate shows the two fates of one glucose molecule.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — hexagon on left (glucose); two horizontal tracks branching: upper track labeled 'oxidation → 30 ATP'; lower track labeled 'glycolysis → 2 ATP + building blocks'. Track colors VERM upper, GREEN lower.

beats.role_note: Stakes before the build — the reprogramming is intentional
beats.narration_text: The upper track burns glucose for energy. The lower track uses it as carbon to build more cell. That building material is what growing cells actually need. The Warburg effect is not inefficiency — it is an intentional reprogramming of glucose fate.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — annotation: 'cancer cells need carbon, not ATP' with arrow pointing to building-block cluster; 'Warburg = reprogramming, not a broken furnace'

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — the REAL Claude Code prompt. greeting = 'The ask,'
beats.narration_text: The ask. Into Claude: port the warburg-carbon plate from plates underscore gen dot py p03 into Manim. Hexagon input in BLUE with ORANGE stroke. Two horizontal tracks branching from it — upper track has three VERM nodes ending in a large ORANGE ATP square; lower track has three GREEN nodes ending in building blocks — a triangle, a rectangle, a rod in SKY — plus a small ORANGE ATP square and one excreted circle to the right. Animate: reveal hexagon, branch both tracks, reveal end-states.

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — the ACTUAL B05_WarburgCarbon class, trimmed to what teaches
beats.narration_text: Read it. The hexagon is a RegularPolygon of six sides. Two tracks branch from it — each track is a list of node positions and a color. The ATP squares are plain Squares; the size contrast is the whole point: large square for thirty ATP, small square for two. The building block cluster is three shapes assembled at the track terminus. LaggedStart for nodes, GrowArrow for track arrows, FadeIn for end-states. The Flash on the hexagon is the punctuation.

props.title: scenes.py — B05_WarburgCarbon
props.code:
# scenes.py — Claude Code output
BLUE="#0072B2"; ORANGE="#E69F00"; GREEN="#009E73"
VERM="#D55E00"; SKY="#56B4E9"; GRAY="#7c7c7c"

class B05_WarburgCarbon(Scene):
  def construct(self):
    hx=RegularPolygon(n=6,color=BLUE,fill_color=BLUE,
      fill_opacity=0.18,stroke_width=4).scale(0.7).move_to([-5.5,0,0])
    # upper track (VERM nodes → large ATP)
    u_nodes=VGroup(*[RoundedRectangle(
      width=1.0,height=0.65,corner_radius=0.12,
      color=VERM,fill_color=VERM,fill_opacity=0.16,
      stroke_width=3.2).move_to([-3.0+i*2.2,1.4,0]) for i in range(3)])
    atp_lg=Square(side_length=1.3,color=ORANGE,
      fill_color=ORANGE,fill_opacity=0.7).move_to([3.2,1.4,0])
    # lower track (GREEN nodes → building blocks + small ATP)
    l_nodes=VGroup(*[RoundedRectangle(
      width=1.0,height=0.65,corner_radius=0.12,
      color=GREEN,fill_color=GREEN,fill_opacity=0.16,
      stroke_width=3.2).move_to([-3.0+i*2.2,-1.4,0]) for i in range(3)])
    atp_sm=Square(side_length=0.55,color=ORANGE,
      fill_color=ORANGE,fill_opacity=0.7).move_to([3.2,-1.4,0])
    # choreography
    self.play(FadeIn(hx),run_time=0.5)
    self.play(LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(n) for n in u_nodes],
              lag_ratio=0.2,run_time=1.1))
    self.play(LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(n) for n in l_nodes],
              lag_ratio=0.2,run_time=1.1))
    self.play(FadeIn(atp_lg),FadeIn(atp_sm),run_time=0.6)
    self.play(Flash(hx.get_center(),color=ORANGE,
              line_length=0.3,num_lines=14,flash_radius=0.9))
    self.wait(0.8)

beats.role_note: Manim render of B05_WarburgCarbon — watch the two tracks and ATP size contrast
beats.narration_text: Run it. Hexagon in. Upper track reveals left to right — three VERM nodes. Lower track reveals — three GREEN nodes. Then the end-states arrive: one large ATP square on top, one small ATP square on the bottom, plus a cluster of building blocks. The Flash on the hexagon closes the loop — same input, two destinations. That size gap between the ATP squares is the entire Warburg effect in one frame.

The change. Revise: add ORANGE dot particles flowing along each track lane — dots traveling from nodes toward endpoints. Large ATP square grows from small to full size with a scale animation. Building blocks assemble one piece at a time. Flash both ATP squares so the size contrast has a beat.

beats.narration_text: Watch the revision. Particles flow down both lanes — the glucose is moving. The large ATP square grows from a seed — you watch it become large. The building blocks assemble piece by piece. Then both ATP squares flash: one is large, one is tiny. Two destinations from one starting molecule. The motion made the contrast physical.

Two destinations from one starting molecule. The motion made the contrast physical: one big ATP square versus one small one, and a pile of building blocks. That size gap is the whole Warburg effect in one frame. Claude ported the hexagon, two track lanes, and the end-state shapes in one prompt. The revision animated the flow and made the scale contrast kinetic.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — summary card: 'Warburg = carbon routing'; two ATP squares side by side (large vs small); 'the size gap is the teaching point'

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read aloud AND discussed. greeting = 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt into Claude: add a third fate — a dashed branch from the hexagon that goes nowhere, labeled 'blocked oxidation.' Then animate a PET-scan proxy: a bright ORANGE glow that expands outward from the hexagon when the lower glycolysis track is active. Why run it? Because the PET-scan sees glucose uptake — the glow is exactly what an FDG-PET scan is detecting. The animation connects the plate geometry to the clinical tool in one visual.

Then after the lower track reveals, play an expanding ORANGE glow from the
hexagon to simulate FDG-PET signal — glycolysis active = glucose trapping."
